sections.body: AI is no longer a side project in this industry. The regulators now expect a documented case for every model that touches a submission, a batch record or a safety decision, so the work that matters most is governance: knowing which models are in use, what each is trusted to do, and how that trust was established.
sections.heading: What it means for a life sciences team

explainer:
Life sciences covers the companies that discover, develop, make and sell medicines, vaccines, diagnostics and medical devices: pharmaceutical and biotechnology firms, medtech makers, and the contract research and manufacturing organisations that work for them. It is one of the most regulated industries in the world, and that shapes how AI is used in it more than anything else.

A medicine moves through a long chain before it reaches a patient. Scientists choose a biological target, design and test molecules, run preclinical studies, then three phases of clinical trials. Regulators review the evidence, the product is manufactured under Good Manufacturing Practice, marketed under strict promotional rules, and watched for safety problems for as long as it is sold. AI now appears at every one of those steps, but the rules for using it differ sharply between them.

The dividing line is whether an AI system influences a regulated decision. A model that helps a chemist brainstorm molecules is a research tool. A model whose output a regulator relies on, to select trial patients, release a batch or judge a safety signal, must be shown to be credible and controlled, documented and monitored like any other validated system. Most of the hard work in life sciences AI is on that second side of the line.

The sections below follow the lifecycle: discovery, clinical development, regulation and quality, manufacturing, safety, medical writing, commercial work, medical devices, and how companies adopt and govern AI across all of it.
key_points: AI is used across the whole medicine lifecycle, from target discovery to post-market safety.
Regulators judge AI by its context of use: the more a regulated decision depends on a model, the more evidence it needs.
The FDA, the EMA and the EU AI Act now set concrete expectations rather than general principles.
The first AI derived medicines have produced clinical results, but none has yet completed phase 3.
The companies reporting real gains treat AI as a governed change programme, not a software purchase.
